seo_title: Can You Invoke Appraisal After a Denied Claim in Texas?
meta_description: Can you invoke appraisal after a denied claim? Learn when a Texas denial is really an amount-of-loss dispute and how to demand it.
h1: Can You Invoke Appraisal After a Denied Claim?
secondary_keywords: coverage dispute vs amount of loss
excerpt: Many denials are really disputes over how much damage exists. Learn when Texas homeowners can still invoke appraisal after a denied claim and when they cannot.
key_takeaways: Appraisal decides amount of loss, not whether the policy covers the loss.
Below-deductible and partial denials are often amount-of-loss disputes appraisal can resolve.
State Farm Lloyds v. Johnson lets appraisers assess causation tied to extent of damage.
Read the denial reason closely and act before deadlines run.
body_html:
You can often invoke appraisal after a denied claim, but it depends on why the claim was denied. If the insurer says the damage is below your deductible or limited to a few items, that is usually an amount-of-loss dispute appraisal can resolve. If it denies coverage entirely under an exclusion, appraisal generally cannot decide that question.

A denial letter feels final. Many Texas homeowners read "your claim has been denied" and assume there is nothing left to do. In reality, many denials are not true coverage denials at all. They are disagreements about how much damage the storm caused, written in the language of a denial.

This guide explains what appraisal can and cannot decide, how to read a denial letter, the Texas law that shapes the answer, and the steps to take if your claim was denied but you still believe covered damage exists.

What Can Insurance Appraisal Decide?

The appraisal clause in most Texas homeowners and commercial property policies applies when you and the insurer "fail to agree on the amount of loss." Each side appoints an appraiser, the appraisers select an umpire, and an award signed by any two of the three generally sets the amount of loss. Our guide to what an insurance appraisal is covers the basics.

Appraisal usually decides:

  • The cost to repair or replace damaged property
  • The scope of repairs needed
  • Whether specific damage was caused by the covered event (for example, which shingles hail damaged)
  • Pricing, quantities, and replacement cost versus actual cash value figures

Appraisal usually does not decide:

  • Whether the policy covers a type of loss at all
  • Whether an exclusion applies, such as flood, wear and tear, or long-term leakage
  • Whether the policy was in force or conditions were met
  • Bad faith or extra-contractual claims

Coverage Denial vs Amount-of-Loss Dispute

The key question is what kind of "denial" you received.

Denial reason in the letterType of disputeAppraisal likely available?
"Damage does not exceed your deductible"Amount of lossOften yes
"Only minor damage found; repair, not replacement"Amount and extent of lossOften yes
"Hail damage limited to soft metals; roof not damaged"Extent of damage / causationOften yes
"Damage caused by wear and tear, not the storm"Causation, may overlap coverageSometimes, depends on facts
"Flood excluded" or "loss caused by long-term leak"CoverageGenerally no
"Policy lapsed" or "late notice"Coverage / policy conditionsGenerally no

A "below deductible" letter is technically a denial of payment, but the insurer is really saying the amount of loss is small. If your contractor's estimate is well above the deductible, you and the insurer disagree about the amount, which is what appraisal is designed to settle.

What Texas Law Says About Appraisal After a Denial

The leading Texas case is State Farm Lloyds v. Johnson (Tex. 2009). There, the insurer agreed some hail damage existed but disputed how much of the roof the hail damaged. The Texas Supreme Court held that appraisers can decide the amount of loss and may assess causation as it relates to the extent of damage, while coverage and liability remain for the insurer and the courts.

In practical terms, if the insurer admits a covered event caused at least some damage, a dispute about how much damage that event caused is generally appraisable. If the insurer denies that any covered peril caused the loss, the question looks more like coverage, and appraisal may not resolve it on its own.

This is general information, not legal advice. Policy wording varies, and a Texas attorney can advise you on a specific denial.

Tip: Read the denial letter for the exact reason, not just the word "denied." Highlight every sentence that mentions amounts, estimates, deductibles, or the extent of damage. Those are signs of an amount-of-loss dispute.

Claims Where Appraisal Is Often Invoked After a Denial

Hail-damaged roofs

Hail claims are the most common example in Texas. The adjuster finds dents on gutters and vents but calls the shingles undamaged or the damage cosmetic, then issues a "below deductible" letter. If you have evidence of functional shingle damage, the dispute often belongs in appraisal. See insurance appraisal for hail damage claims.

Wind damage

Insurers sometimes approve a handful of replacement shingles and deny the rest. Whether the roof can be repaired or must be replaced is an extent-of-damage question.

Water damage

Water claims are trickier, because exclusions for long-term seepage or maintenance often drive the denial. When the insurer accepts a sudden discharge but disputes the extent of damage, appraisal may apply.

Fire and smoke

Fire coverage is rarely denied outright, but insurers may refuse to pay for smoke cleaning or replacement in rooms they consider unaffected. That extent dispute can be appraisable.

How to Read a Denial Letter

  1. Identify the stated reason. Is it an exclusion, a policy condition, or a finding about damage and amounts?
  2. Find the policy provisions cited. Compare them to the actual policy language.
  3. Check whether any damage was accepted. Partial acceptance often signals an amount dispute.
  4. Request the adjuster's estimate, photos, and any engineer report. You are entitled to understand the basis for the decision.
  5. Note deadlines. Policies and Texas law impose time limits; our Texas claim deadline calculator can help you track them.

Texas Insurance Code chapter 542 requires insurers to notify you in writing of the reasons for rejecting a claim. The Texas Department of Insurance also accepts complaints if you believe a claim was mishandled.

How the Appraisal Process Works After a Denied Claim

  1. Policy and denial review. Confirm the policy has an appraisal clause and that the dispute concerns amount or extent of loss.
  2. Written demand. Send a written appraisal demand that names your appraiser, as the clause requires.
  3. Appraiser selection. The insurer names its appraiser, typically within a set time stated in the policy.
  4. Umpire selection. The two appraisers agree on an umpire, or either side may ask a court to appoint one.
  5. Inspection and estimate exchange. The appraisers inspect, exchange line-item estimates, and negotiate.
  6. Award. Agreement by both appraisers, or one appraiser and the umpire, produces a signed award.

Our article on what happens after invoking the appraisal clause in Texas walks through each step in more detail.

What happens to the coverage question?

Insurers sometimes agree to appraisal while reserving their coverage defenses. That means the appraisal award can set the amount of loss, but the insurer may still argue that some or all of it is not covered. Understanding that possibility up front prevents surprises.

Mistakes Homeowners Make After a Denied Claim

  • Assuming denial ends the claim. Many denials are disputes about amounts that can be challenged.
  • Waiting too long. Delay can raise waiver arguments and lets damage worsen. Texas weather claims also carry pre-suit notice requirements under chapter 542A.
  • Failing to document. Photos, dated storm reports, and independent estimates matter. Use our claim documentation checklist.
  • Making permanent repairs before documenting. Temporary repairs to prevent further damage are fine; complete repairs can erase evidence.
  • Confusing appraisal with litigation. Appraisal resolves amount of loss; it does not replace legal advice on coverage or bad faith.

What to Look for in an Appraiser After a Denial

Denied claims are some of the hardest to appraise, because your appraiser has to prove not only what repairs cost but that the damage exists and was caused by the covered event. Look for someone who brings:

  • Field inspection experience with hail, wind, water, and fire losses, so they can identify and document damage the adjuster missed.
  • Detailed estimating skills in Xactimate or Symbility, since the award is built line by line.
  • Familiarity with Texas appraisal practice, including how umpires are chosen and how causation is handled after Johnson.
  • Independence, meaning no stake in performing the repairs.
  • Clear communication about whether your dispute is truly appraisable before you spend money on it.

Joseph Dittman has spent his career on the policyholder side of Texas property claims as a licensed public adjuster, inspecting losses and negotiating with carrier adjusters. On an appraisal assignment, he serves as your appraiser only. Across Texas, from Waco to Dallas, Austin, and Houston, denied hail and wind claims are among the most common disputes he reviews, often after spring storms leave carriers handling large volumes of claims in a short window.

Appraisal vs Lawsuit After a Denied Claim

Appraisal is usually faster and less expensive than litigation when the dispute is about how much damage exists. When the insurer flatly denies coverage, an attorney may be the right first call. Some claims involve both: appraisal sets the number, while coverage questions are handled separately. Our guide to whether you can sue after insurance appraisal explains how the two interact in Texas.

Cost matters too. Under most appraisal clauses, each side pays its own appraiser and the two sides split the umpire's fee. Before invoking appraisal, compare that expense to the realistic difference between the insurer's position and the true cost of repairs. If the gap is small, a well-documented reinspection request or supplement may be the better first step.

Next Steps If Your Claim Was Denied

  • Get the denial letter, adjuster's estimate, and photos in writing.
  • Determine whether the reason is coverage or amount.
  • Gather independent evidence of the damage and its cause.
  • Review your policy's appraisal clause and deadlines.
  • Get an experienced opinion before sending a demand.

faqs.q: Is a below-deductible letter a claim denial?
faqs.a: It works like one, because no payment is issued, but it is really a finding about the amount of loss. The insurer is saying damage costs less than your deductible. If your contractor or appraiser estimates the covered damage well above the deductible, you and the insurer disagree on the amount, which is generally the kind of dispute appraisal is designed to resolve.

faqs.q: Can the insurance company refuse my appraisal demand after a denial?
faqs.a: An insurer may refuse if it believes the dispute is purely about coverage, such as an excluded peril or a lapsed policy. If the disagreement is about how much damage a covered event caused, Texas courts generally treat it as appraisable. When an insurer refuses a proper demand, policyholders sometimes ask a court to compel appraisal. Talk to an attorney about your options.

faqs.q: How long do I have to invoke appraisal after a denied claim?
faqs.a: It depends on your policy and the facts. Some policies set specific timelines, and unreasonable delay can lead an insurer to argue you waived appraisal. Texas also has suit limitation periods and a 61-day pre-suit notice requirement for weather claims under chapter 542A. Review your policy promptly and act as soon as you know the dispute will not resolve.

faqs.q: Will appraisal overturn a coverage denial?
faqs.a: No. Appraisal sets the amount of loss, not whether the policy covers it. If the insurer denies coverage under an exclusion, an appraisal award does not override that decision. An insurer may also participate in appraisal while reserving coverage defenses. Coverage disputes are typically handled through further negotiation, a TDI complaint, or legal action.

faqs.q: Should I hire an appraiser or an attorney after a denial?
faqs.a: If the dispute is about the amount or extent of damage, an experienced appraiser is often the more efficient choice. If the insurer denies coverage outright or you suspect bad faith, consult a Texas attorney. Some claims involve both, with appraisal setting the number and an attorney addressing coverage. A free claim review can help clarify which path fits.
